A_target.statement:
Let $X$ be a [[Definition:Banach Space|Banach space]].
Let $M$ be a [[Definition:Closed Linear Subspace|closed linear subspace]] of $X$.
Then $X / M$ is a [[Definition:Banach Space|Banach space]] under the [[Definition:Quotient Norm|quotient norm]]:
:$\displaystyle \norm {x + M} = \inf_{m \mathop \in M} \norm {x - m}$

B_source.statement:
Let $T: X \to Y$ be a [[Definition:Linear Transformation|linear transformation]] of [[Definition:Vector Space|vector spaces]].
Then:
:$X / \map \ker T \cong \Img T$

substitutions.the linear map T: a bounded linear map with kernel M

derived.the induced isomorphism: an isometric isomorphism onto the image when T is a quotient map

object_map.reformulation: The purely algebraic quotient must be equipped with a norm before the isomorphism theorem has analytic content; closedness of the subspace is exactly what makes that possible.

validity_conditions: M must be closed for the quotient norm to be a norm rather than a seminorm
completeness of X is needed for completeness of the quotient, proved via absolutely convergent series
the isomorphism is topological only when the map is open, which is guaranteed for the canonical projection
proof_plan:
Define $\norm {x + M} = \map d {x, M}$, the [[Definition:Distance to Set|distance]] from any representative to $M$.
This does not depend on the representative.

[[Definition:Norm Axioms|Homogeneity]] and the [[Triangle Inequality]] follow from those of $\norm \cdot$.
If $\norm {x + M} = 0$, then $x \in \overline M = M$ as $M$ is [[Definition:Closed Set (Metric Space)|closed]], so $x + M = 0$.

Let $\displaystyle \sum_n \norm {x_n + M} < \infty$.
Choose $y_n \in x_n + M$ with $\norm {y_n} < \norm {x_n + M} + 2^{-n}$.
Then $\sum_n y_n$ converges in $X$ as $X$ is [[Definition:Banach Space|Banach]], and its class is the sum of $\sum_n \paren {x_n + M}$.
By [[Absolutely Convergent Series in Normed Vector Space is Convergent iff Space is Banach]], $X / M$ is complete.

Let $\pi: X \to X / M$ be the [[Definition:Quotient Mapping|canonical map]].
Then $\map \ker \pi = M$, and by the algebraic isomorphism theorem $X / \map \ker \pi \cong \Img \pi = X / M$.

We have $
orm {\map \pi x} \le 
orm x$, so $
orm \pi \le 1$.
The open unit ball of $X$ maps onto the open unit ball of $X / M$, so $\pi$ is an [[Definition:Open Mapping|open mapping]].
{{qed}}
